a3114.speech: Sent an email to federal workers asking “what did you do last week?” and several times said a failure to respond would be tantamount to a resignation.

a3114.speaker: Twenty-one United States Digital Service technology staffers (resignation)
a3114.name: Twenty-one United States Digital Service technology staffers (resignation)
a3114.speech: Complained of hostile interviews from DOGE employees and said that in the current extreme circumstances they could no longer honor their oaths to serve the people and uphold the Constitution.

a3114.speaker: Paul Barrett, deputy director of the Center for Business and Human Rights at New York University’s Stern School of Business
a3114.name: Paul Barrett
a3114.title: deputy director of the Center for Business and Human Rights at New York University’s Stern School of Business
a3114.speech: Said that the symbolic value of the resignations of public servants who intimately understand the government’s operating systems would outstrip any operational risk their departures posed. “The federal government is a big workforce, a couple of million. So, 20 people leaving is not going to change the situation in some dramatic way. What’s important here is that, like some of their brother and sister civil servants who have resigned or been willing to be fired rather than cooperating with the Musk-DOGE rampage, these people are saying, ‘We will not cooperate. We will not obey. This is not legitimate.’”

a3114.speaker: US District Judge Loren AliKhan
a3114.name: US District Judge Loren AliKhan
a3114.speech: “Defendants’ actions were irrational, imprudent, and precipitated a nationwide crisis.”

a3114.speaker: Elizabeth Glidden, fired technical program officer in USAID’s Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance
a3114.name: Elizabeth Glidden
a3114.title: fired technical program officer in USAID’s Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance
a3114.speech: “Our goal is to just start putting some faces and names to all the federal workers who have been impacted by the furloughs, layoffs, immediate firings by Musk and DOGE.” ; “It’s been terrible. I’ve cried everyday. I go through waves of crying, anger, frustration.”

a3114.speaker: Several House Republicans
a3114.name: Several House Republicans
a3114.speech: Pleaded with leadership Tuesday for guidance on handling a deluge of questions from constituents about recent cuts.

a3114.speaker: Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, New York Republican
a3114.name: Rep. Nicole Malliotakis
a3114.title: New York Republican
a3114.speech: Said Trump had appointed “very smart people” as Cabinet secretaries and they should be empowered to make cuts. “This idea that they were going to just fire people via Twitter, Elon Musk, that to me, seems rash.”

a3114.speaker: Mike Johnson, House Speaker, Louisiana Republican
a3114.name: Mike Johnson
a3114.title: House Speaker, Louisiana Republican
a3114.speech: “I think the vast majority of the American people understand and applaud and appreciate the DOGE effort, the goal to scale down the size and scope of government.”

a3114.speaker: John Thune, GOP Senate Majority Leader
a3114.name: John Thune
a3114.title: GOP Senate Majority Leader
a3114.speech: Was more mindful of the humanity of the federal workers let go, while sharing the goal of trimming government, saying “It needs to be done in a respectful way.”

a3114.speaker: Paul Barrett, deputy director of the Center for Business and Human Rights at New York University’s Stern School of Business
a3114.name: Paul Barrett
a3114.title: deputy director of the Center for Business and Human Rights at New York University’s Stern School of Business
a3114.speech: Believes that significant political pressure on even a small number of GOP members in Congress could slow the DOGE purge: “I think there’s every chance in the world that a handful of members of Congress will summon the courage to confront Trump and suffer his wrath if they get enough constituents back home telling them ‘Hey, we sent you to Washington and we’ve had enough of this. This is this is chaos, craziness.’”

a3301.speaker: Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade
a3301.name: Ministry of Commerce
a3301.title: Industry and Trade
a3301.speech: Confirmed the announcement that from November 1, 2025, the price of an 800-gram loaf of white bread will increase from E16.73 to E17.90, while brown bread of the same size will cost E15.60, up from E14.58 ; said the increase follows a request submitted in April this year by the Eswatini Bakers' Association (EBA).

a3301.speaker: Members of the public / consumers (interviewed, unnamed)
a3301.name: Members of the public / consumers (interviewed
a3301.title: unnamed)
a3301.speech: Say the hike will translate into a heavy financial blow for thousands of households already battling rising costs of food, fuel and transport, and accuse government of ignoring the plight of the poor; several residents described the adjustment as a huge blow to those who live from hand to mouth.

a3301.speaker: One consumer (anonymous)
a3301.name: One consumer (anonymous)
a3301.speech: "I was shocked to hear about the increase. We are already struggling to buy basic groceries. For the poor, this is not just about bread, it's about survival."

a3301.speaker: Another consumer in Mbabane (anonymous)
a3301.name: Another consumer in Mbabane (anonymous)
a3301.speech: Said the hike showed a lack of empathy from policymakers: "The timing is terrible. The cost of everything is up and now they are raising bread prices again. Government should have found another way to support bakeries without punishing consumers."

a3301.speaker: A resident of Simunye (anonymous)
a3301.name: A resident of Simunye (anonymous)
a3301.speech: "Every Lilangeni counts. When the price of bread goes up, it affects everyone, especially those earning below E2 000 a month. It means skipping breakfast or sending a child to school on an empty stomach."

a3301.speaker: A consumer from Nhlangano (anonymous)
a3301.name: A consumer from Nhlangano (anonymous)
a3301.speech: "It's becoming a cycle. Every time the cost of living goes up, we are told it's because of rising input costs. However, we never see the same energy to protect consumers or increase wages for private-sector workers."

a3301.speaker: Another consumer from Mbabane (anonymous)
a3301.name: Another consumer from Mbabane (anonymous)
a3301.speech: "We are not all civil servants. We didn't get the raise. Now those who didn't benefit from the salary review will be hit even harder."

a3301.speaker: Eswatini Bakers' Association (EBA)
a3301.name: Eswatini Bakers' Association (EBA)
a3301.speech: Argued that sustained rises in production costs were threatening the survival of bakeries across the country.

a3301.speaker: Central Bank of Eswatini (CBE), August/September 2025 Monthly Statistical Report
a3301.name: Central Bank of Eswatini (CBE)
a3301.title: August/September 2025 Monthly Statistical Report
a3301.speech: Reported that the total credit given to households and non-profit groups (NPISH) reached E8.8 billion in August 2025, a rise of one per cent compared to the previous month and a 2.8 per cent growth year-on-year, driven by a 2.6 per cent increase in car loans, which reached E1.3 billion: "There was also a two per cent rise in unsecured personal loans (like bank overdrafts or simple personal loans), bringing that total to E3.3 billion" ; mortgage loans declined by 0.2 per cent, standing at E4.2 billion, while ordinary savings deposits increased by one per cent, reaching E2.1 billion.

a3301.speaker: Central Statistical Office (CSO), Consumer Price Index
a3301.name: Central Statistical Office (CSO)
a3301.title: Consumer Price Index
a3301.speech: Showed the country's annual inflation rate rose slightly to 2.8 per cent in September from 2.6 per cent recorded in August 2025.

a3301.speaker: World Economic Outlook
a3301.name: World Economic Outlook
a3301.speech: Projects the country's growth at 4.3 per cent.

a3301.speaker: News 24 (South Africa)
a3301.name: News 24 (South Africa)
a3301.speech: Reported that key food items saw significant price hikes: tomatoes jumped 26 per cent, carrots 20 per cent, onions 11 per cent and oranges 18 per cent.

a3301.speaker: The economist (unnamed)
a3301.name: The economist (unnamed)
a3301.speech: Said the fact that sectors like gambling and entertainment were growing suggests that consumers are frustrated and seeking an outlet to momentarily 'live' their challenges; said those who gamble are doing so with the illusion or quest of deserting their financial challenges by hitting the 'jackpot', and the same goes for those who imbibe in alcohol, seeking for a moment to neglect their challenges, which include 'black tax' and the skyrocketing cost of living ; "What needs to be considered if the economy is growing and the public is having any money in their pockets are things like the buying of property and cars. Such commodities depict whether money is available for the consumers to engage in huge investments."

a3301.speaker: Unions
a3301.name: Unions
a3301.speech: Call for a minimum wage, claiming their members can barely afford basic commodities.

a3301.speaker: Ministry for Labour and Social Security
a3301.name: Ministry for Labour and Social Security
a3301.speech: Reported that during the quarter under review, a total of 16 redundancies were reported, affecting 2 056 employees, compared to six redundancies involving 133 employees in 2024 and 14 redundancies affecting 1 072 employees in 2023, indicating a 63 per cent increase in reported retrenchments ; reported that the sudden surge in redundancies is a result of the United States Presidential Order reducing funding to member States under the PEPFAR Project.

a3892.speaker: Suleyman Mohamud, Somali Attorney General
a3892.name: Suleyman Mohamud
a3892.title: Somali Attorney General
a3892.speech: Wrote to the Banaadir Regional Court on March 22, directing it to drop the case of Abdirashid Janan, who has been accused of killing and torturing civilians. ; Mohamed [Mohamud] informed the court that the government no longer plans to continue prosecution of the man who escaped custody early 2020 after being in the hands of government for months.

a3892.speaker: Banaadir Regional Court (response letter to the Attorney General seen by Horn Observer)
a3892.name: Banaadir Regional Court (response letter to the Attorney General seen by Horn Observer)
a3892.speech: The court announced pardoned of the offenses he allegedly committed in Gedo region of southern Somalia.

a3892.speaker: Nicolas Berlanga, EU ambassador to Somalia
a3892.name: Nicolas Berlanga
a3892.title: EU ambassador to Somalia
a3892.speech: Said the embrace of Janan by the Federal Government was aimed at achieving 'short term gains' in violation of rights of Janan's victims.

a3892.speaker: UN Somalia and Eritrea Monitoring Group (SEMG), 2016 and 2017 reports
a3892.name: UN Somalia and Eritrea Monitoring Group (SEMG)
a3892.title: 2016 and 2017 reports
a3892.speech: Accused Janan of serious human rights violations, and of "conduct constituting obstruction of humanitarian assistance" between 2014 and 2017.

a3892.speaker: Amnesty International
a3892.name: Amnesty International
a3892.speech: Last month, called on Somalia's federal government to ensure Janan faced accountability for alleged human rights violations he committed in Gedo while he was a security minister. "Now that Abdirashid Janan is in the hands of the federal government of Somalia, authorities must ensure justice and accountability for all the alleged human rights violations he committed in Gedo. Victims and impacted families deserve justice."

a3892.speaker: Somali government
a3892.name: Somali government
a3892.speech: The Somali government paraded dozens of captured Jubaland fighters after the January 25 battle in Beled Hawo and said close to 100 were taken into custody.

a4005.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (statement)
a4005.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (statement)
a4005.speech: According to an IOM statement, the raids by Islamist terrorists in Cabo Delgado have forced the displacement of about 60,000 people in two weeks; the escalating attacks that began on 20 July displaced 57,034 people, or 13,343 households, and Chiúre “was the hardest-hit district, with more than 42,000 people uprooted, more than half of them children.”

a4005.speaker: Paola Emerson, head of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in Mozambique
a4005.name: Paola Emerson
a4005.title: head of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in Mozambique
a4005.speech: “So far, around 30,000 displaced people have received food, water, shelter, and essential household items. However, the response is not yet at the scale required to meet growing needs” ; said the slashing reductions of foreign aid by the Trump regime in the United States and by other international bodies makes it difficult for aid organizations to meet the requirements of those in need ; “Funding cuts mean life-saving aid is being scaled back” ; “The lack of safety and documentation, and involuntary relocations, are worsening the situation”.

a4035.speaker: Malawi Congress Party (MCP) 2025-2030 manifesto
a4035.name: Malawi Congress Party (MCP) 2025-2030 manifesto
a4035.speech: Proposes to ban foreign governments from channelling aid to agencies outside the government channels, and further proposes publication of annual reports detailing foreign aid pledges and disbursement status to ensure that foreign aid is provided solely through government channels purportedly to respect the country's sovereignty and democratic principles.

a4035.speaker: Benedicto Kondowe, human rights activist and National Advocacy Platform executive director
a4035.name: Benedicto Kondowe
a4035.title: human rights activist and National Advocacy Platform executive director
a4035.speech: Condemned the move, stating that it would centralise all donor aid under State control. He said direct funding from foreign governments is crucial for CSOs to hold the government accountable, reach marginalised populations and enable citizen participation without political interference. Said Kondowe: "The clause signals bad faith. It smacks of an attempt to financially suffocate and discipline CSOs behind patriotic rhetoric. Forcing all aid through government invites politicisation, delays, and the silencing of dissent which strains constitutional rights to association and participation." He said Malawi already has oversight mechanisms, including foreign exchange regulations and the Non-Governmental Organisations (NGO) Act that sufficiently monitor such resources.

a4035.speaker: Charles Kajoloweka, Youth and Society (YAS) executive director
a4035.name: Charles Kajoloweka
a4035.title: Youth and Society (YAS) executive director
a4035.speech: Condemned the proposal outright, calling it a "blatant attempt to undermine civic space". He said: "The proposal in the MCP manifesto to ban funding for NGOs is not only delusional and simplistic, but also a blatant attempt to undermine civic space. This is a new weapon of choice for authoritarian regimes across the globe to undermine critical civic society by restricting funding from foreign sources."

a4035.speaker: Willy Kambwandira, Centre for Social Accountability and Transparency executive director
a4035.name: Willy Kambwandira
a4035.title: Centre for Social Accountability and Transparency executive director
a4035.speech: Said the broader implications of the proposal are that it may affect the independence of CSOs and lead to the suppression of dissenting views of CSOs.

a4035.speaker: George Chaima, political analyst
a4035.name: George Chaima
a4035.title: political analyst
a4035.speech: Described the proposal as a sign of oppression which could also discourage donors from supporting Malawi.

a4035.speaker: Wonderful Mkutche, political analyst
a4035.name: Wonderful Mkutche
a4035.title: political analyst
a4035.speech: Pointed out that foreign governments tend to prefer direct funding to CSOs because they distrust government transparency, further warning that such a policy could create hostility between the government and CSOs, potentially shrinking civic space further.

a4035.speaker: Jessie Kabwira, MCP spokesperson; Moses Kunkuyu, campaign director; and Richard Chimwendo Banda, secretary general (non-response)
a4035.name: Jessie Kabwira
a4035.title: MCP spokesperson; Moses Kunkuyu, campaign director; and Richard Chimwendo Banda, secretary general (non-response)
a4035.speech: Could not be reached as their phones went unanswered.

a4035.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a4035.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a4035.title: President of Malawi
a4035.speech: Pledged ambitious reforms at the manifesto launch, including the creation of three million jobs for the youth, the transformation of the National Economic Empowerment Fund into a development bank and the Tsogolo Account, which promises K500 000 savings for all children born in Malawi to be accessed upon turning 18 years of age.

a4221.speaker: Beyene Russom, Eritrea’s Ambassador to Kenya
a4221.name: Beyene Russom
a4221.title: Eritrea’s Ambassador to Kenya
a4221.speech: Highlighting the deep meaning of Eritrean independence and the heavy sacrifice paid, expressed appreciation to all who contributed to the colorful event.

a4221.speaker: Robel Aaron, chairman of the Eritrean community in Finland
a4221.name: Robel Aaron
a4221.title: chairman of the Eritrean community in Finland
a4221.speech: Emphasized the heavy sacrifices made for independence and called on nationals to strengthen their organizational capacity and participation in national affairs; he also urged the transfer of noble societal values to future generations.

a4221.speaker: Eritrean nationals in Minnesota and Orange County, United States
a4221.name: Eritrean nationals in Minnesota and Orange County
a4221.title: United States
a4221.speech: Expressed their readiness to play their due part in the successful implementation of national development programs.

a4275.speaker: Gloria Magombo, Energy and Power Development ministry permanent secretary
a4275.name: Gloria Magombo
a4275.title: Energy and Power Development ministry permanent secretary
a4275.speech: Says Zimbabwe's electricity access rate has risen to 62 percent, from 53 percent in 2020, and said the government is now pushing for the country to have access to modern energy. "So, you would see that for rural communities and in a country like ours… access to modern energy, particularly electricity, is around 62 percent. We still have 38 percent of the population who do not have access to modern energy, and that is a critical challenge for us as a government," she said ; "We are working quite hard to ensure that we achieve the vision that we have for this country. So, the 38 percent we are talking about, we are transitioning from basic traditional fuels to modern energy." ; She said there is a need to ensure the viability and affordability of energy services: "Others are transitioning from using things like paraffin lamps to at least modern lamps that are solar or battery enabled, so there are a lot of different stories to transition, but what is critical for all of us is that they should be affordable and clean."

a4275.speaker: African Development Bank
a4275.name: African Development Bank
a4275.speech: Highlighted in July 2019 that the country needs US$34 billion over the next decade to restore its road, rail, aviation, energy, information communication and technology and water and sanitation infrastructure to proper working conditions.

a4780.speaker: Dr Boa Jacques, doctor (Odontostomatology/Maxillofacial Surgery department, CHR of Fada)
a4780.name: Dr Boa Jacques
a4780.title: doctor (Odontostomatology/Maxillofacial Surgery department, CHR of Fada)
a4780.speech: According to him, a significant need remains unmet in the treatment of disfiguring conditions, which are often neglected by traditional humanitarian aid ; "These conditions seriously compromise the social reintegration and psychological well-being of patients. It is therefore essential to mobilise more resources and to raise NGOs' awareness of this problem. The current security context constitutes a major obstacle to access to care. Yet, with appropriate support, significant potential remains untapped to help a greater number of people."

a4828.speaker: Justice James Omotosho, Federal High Court, Abuja
a4828.name: Justice James Omotosho
a4828.title: Federal High Court, Abuja
a4828.speech: declared that the notion of a "shadow government" or alternative cabinet "is alien to the Nigerian Constitution and has no legal basis" ; held: "Section 14(2)(c) makes no allowance for a shadow government. The defendant cannot import foreign constitutional models to confuse Nigerians. Such a so-called shadow government is hereby declared null and void" ; emphasised that the proposal conflicts with Nigeria's presidential system and has the potential to mislead the public, noting that the Constitution does not provide for any parallel or alternative government outside the one it establishes ; acknowledged that the defendant is entitled to his fundamental rights but emphasised that these rights are not absolute and must operate within constitutional limits, concluding that the formation of a shadow government exceeds those limits and is capable of causing societal disruption.

a4828.speaker: State Security Service (SSS)/Department of State Services (DSS), Nigeria's domestic intelligence agency
a4828.name: State Security Service (SSS)/Department of State Services (DSS)
a4828.title: Nigeria's domestic intelligence agency
a4828.speech: filed a lawsuit challenging Utomi's plan to form a shadow government, describing it as unconstitutional, and sought to prevent Utomi and his associates from pursuing the initiative.

a4828.speaker: Pat Utomi, political economist and former presidential aspirant
a4828.name: Pat Utomi
a4828.title: political economist and former presidential aspirant
a4828.speech: opposed the suit, arguing that his plan fell within his constitutional rights to freedom of expression and association, and that stopping it would infringe on those rights.

a4828.speaker: Seven senior lawyers invited as amici curiae
a4828.name: Seven senior lawyers invited as amici curiae
a4828.speech: submissions from the legal experts were sharply divided at the July 10 hearing: some supported the DSS's stance, while others defended Utomi's proposal as a legitimate civic initiative.

a4882.speaker: Dr. Romain Babagbeto, head of the USAID "Play to Learn" project
a4882.name: Dr. Romain Babagbeto
a4882.title: head of the USAID "Play to Learn" project
a4882.speech: During the opening ceremony of the workshop, underlined the crucial importance of this event in strengthening institutional capacities for effective monitoring of the National Child Policy (PNE) indicators; he also recalled the strong commitment of USAID and Mott MacDonald alongside the Djiboutian government to guarantee broader and more equitable access to quality early childhood education, a primary objective for Djibouti by 2030.

a4882.speaker: Ousman Djama Osman, legal adviser at the Ministry of Women and Family
a4882.name: Ousman Djama Osman
a4882.title: legal adviser at the Ministry of Women and Family
a4882.speech: Speaking on behalf of the Ministry of Women and Family, also stressed the importance of this workshop in ensuring the effectiveness of the PNE: "The National Child Policy is one of the cornerstones of our development. For every child to be able to grow up in a secure environment conducive to their flourishing, we must have reliable indicators to track our progress and adjust our actions according to needs," he pleaded ; "We have the duty, as decision-makers, parents, educators and partners, to guarantee every child a good start in life. The future of our nation depends on it."

a4882.speaker: Ousman Djama Osman, legal adviser at the Ministry of Women and Family
a4882.name: Ousman Djama Osman
a4882.title: legal adviser at the Ministry of Women and Family
a4882.speech: Also highlighted the importance of solid intersectoral collaboration: "Whether you come from education, health or justice, each sector has a crucial role to play. Cooperation between these different fields is the key to ensuring rigorous monitoring of the PNE and to guaranteeing that our efforts converge towards the same objective: the well-being of every Djiboutian child," he specified.

a4882.speaker: Workshop participants (from the education, health and justice sectors)
a4882.name: Workshop participants (from the education
a4882.title: health and justice sectors)
a4882.speech: Validated the indicators collected and proposed adjustments to optimise monitoring; they drew up a clear action plan for the next quarter, including the distribution of responsibilities among stakeholders, and shared their experiences and proposals for improving coordination between the different sectors.

a4907.speaker: Addisu Fekadu (PhD), Associate Professor at Arba Minch University and Enset Project Coordinator
a4907.name: Addisu Fekadu (PhD)
a4907.title: Associate Professor at Arba Minch University and Enset Project Coordinator
a4907.speech: Said that enset is a plant that has been little talked about, yet is used as a staple food by more than 25 million people ; explained that numerous enset-related problems had been brought to Arba Minch University more than ten years earlier and that on that basis the university carried out a survey study.

a4907.speaker: Addisu Fekadu (PhD), Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.name: Addisu Fekadu (PhD)
a4907.title: Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.speech: Said that through the study new decorticating machines were developed and tried out by farmers, and that Ethiopia's first pilot milling station was established at Dorze in Arba Minch town ; added that by developing a starter culture in the laboratory it has been possible to reduce to one week the time the plant takes to become edible ; explained that mothers have been enabled to produce various tourism-oriented products from the enset by-product fibre and bring them to market.

a4907.speaker: Addisu Fekadu (PhD), Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.name: Addisu Fekadu (PhD)
a4907.title: Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.speech: Said that millions of dollars are spent in the country on fertiliser and herbicides to produce wheat, whereas enset requires not a single dollar and no imported input ; explained to Reporter that enset is nutrient-rich, organic and gluten-free and has been quality-certified by international organisations ; said that international food producers have gone beyond showing interest and have taken and tested the product and are requesting to bring it to the international market.

a4907.speaker: Addisu Fekadu (PhD), Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.name: Addisu Fekadu (PhD)
a4907.title: Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.speech: “Because the patent of the machine is ours, we train people in how it is produced. In this way we have distributed the mill to about 20 localities. Now we will soon deliver to 40 localities; our short-term plan is to reach 100,” Addisu (PhD) announced.

a4907.speaker: Addisu Fekadu (PhD), Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.name: Addisu Fekadu (PhD)
a4907.title: Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.speech: Said that in Ethiopia publishing in a well-known journal after research is treated as the final goal, whereas the big goal should be delivering the research to the user, and firmly believes that if that does not happen the budget researchers spend on research should be returned.

a4907.speaker: Tesfaye Habtemariam (PhD), Director General of Research at Arba Minch University
a4907.name: Tesfaye Habtemariam (PhD)
a4907.title: Director General of Research at Arba Minch University
a4907.speech: Said that besides being exhausting, the traditional method of producing enset wastes up to 45 percent of the product, whereas the machine improved and built by Arba Minch University yields up to 98 percent waste-free processing ; explained that a starter culture has been prepared that reduces the two-to-six-month fermentation process to one week.

a4907.speaker: Tesfaye Habtemariam (PhD), Director General of Research at Arba Minch University
a4907.name: Tesfaye Habtemariam (PhD)
a4907.title: Director General of Research at Arba Minch University
a4907.speech: Says confidently that if enset is properly worked on it will solve the country's food problem and also the nutrition problem, and that where it grows it serves like a tree as an option for protecting the environment ; “We spend nothing on chemical fertiliser for enset. We know the amount of foreign currency the country spends on chemical fertiliser. But for enset nothing whatsoever is applied. At most, natural manure might be used,” he explained, holding that this makes a great contribution to the country's economy.

a4907.speaker: Addisu Fekadu (PhD), Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.name: Addisu Fekadu (PhD)
a4907.title: Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.speech: Said that a problem of food utilisation is observed in Ethiopia, that the reports issued every year by the Public Health Institute are alarming, and that it is saddening that children under five are victims of stunting while the country has all this wealth ; “The foods we eat in Ethiopia are few in variety and can be counted on the fingers. Enset contains in abundance the minerals that are said to be deficient in our country. So if we process enset in a modern way and add it to the food system, it will be improved.”

a4907.speaker: Public Health Institute (annual reports)
a4907.name: Public Health Institute (annual reports)
a4907.speech: Cited as issuing alarming annual reports on food utilisation in Ethiopia, including that children under five years of age are victims of stunting.

a4907.speaker: Experts (unnamed)
a4907.name: Experts (unnamed)
a4907.speech: Say that if little-recognised plants found in various parts of the country, such as yam and cassava, were brought into the food system, the benefits obtained would be inexhaustible, and said that otherwise it is dangerous to try to ensure food sovereignty while always importing fertiliser into the country.

a4907.speaker: Addisu Fekadu (PhD), Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.name: Addisu Fekadu (PhD)
a4907.title: Enset Project Coordinator, Arba Minch University
a4907.speech: Commenting on information circulating on social media and other outlets that Ethiopia had achieved food sovereignty, said he too had heard about the matter in the news and that he could not comment in the absence of accurate information on the quantities produced in the various regions, but noted that it is not something one can dare to claim — that self-sufficiency in food has been achieved merely because pulses and cereal crops were produced in quantity.

a4978.speaker: Venuste Ndikumwenayo, director in charge of research and statistics at the Bank of the Republic of Burundi (BRB)
a4978.name: Venuste Ndikumwenayo
a4978.title: director in charge of research and statistics at the Bank of the Republic of Burundi (BRB)
a4978.speech: stressed that "The latter [the clearing house] focuses on facilitating intra-COMESA trade in order to reduce transaction costs for economic operators in the member countries."

a4978.speaker: Venuste Ndikumwenayo, director in charge of research and statistics at the Bank of the Republic of Burundi (BRB)
a4978.name: Venuste Ndikumwenayo
a4978.title: director in charge of research and statistics at the Bank of the Republic of Burundi (BRB)
a4978.speech: indicates that the Burundian economy faces structural rigidities, with imports very high compared with exports, and maintains that Burundi benefits from its membership of COMESA, pointing to the intensification of trade at reduced transaction costs.

a5323.speaker: Yonas Mesganaw, legal advisor at the Authority for Civil Society Organizations (ACSO)
a5323.name: Yonas Mesganaw
a5323.title: legal advisor at the Authority for Civil Society Organizations (ACSO)
a5323.speech: Believes that the bill encourages CSOs to do business without the fear of breaching the agreement.

a5323.speaker: Mesud Gebeyehu, Director of the Consortium of Ethiopian Human Rights Organizations (CEHRO)
a5323.name: Mesud Gebeyehu
a5323.title: Director of the Consortium of Ethiopian Human Rights Organizations (CEHRO)
a5323.speech: Said fund disbursement is related to the relationship between donors and the nation, impacting the acceptance of proposals; said expanding financial sources is the only way his organization will be secured.

a5323.speaker: Abdulaziz Arage, General Director of Kelem Ethiopia
a5323.name: Abdulaziz Arage
a5323.title: General Director of Kelem Ethiopia
a5323.speech: Hopes that commercial banks will include CSOs in their loan portfolio though the bill is a step to alleviate their financial constraints.

a5323.speaker: Study conducted last year (report)
a5323.name: Study conducted last year (report)
a5323.speech: Explained that in 2014, the total funds pledged by CSOs for 2,604 projects, excluding Dire Dewa city, accounted for 35.76 billion Br; the current fund for 2,885 projects under CSOs is committed to 78.87 billion Br; only the Somali and Harari regional states experienced a decline in total budgets as some CSOs did not get the required license to operate.

a5323.speaker: Ahmed Hussien, Director General of Pro Development Network (PDN)
a5323.name: Ahmed Hussien
a5323.title: Director General of Pro Development Network (PDN)
a5323.speech: Said that their organization plans to rent machines that will be functional to dig holes for clean water projects ; “We are contacting donors to get those machines.” ; mentioned that some organizations struggle to get donations, making it difficult to implement their objectives.

a5428.speaker: U.S. Embassy (press release)
a5428.name: U.S. Embassy (press release)
a5428.speech: According to a press release, the U.S. will expand cooperation in mining, energy, technology, and agriculture, due to interventions by the Liberian government in key areas.

a5428.speaker: Joseph Zadrozny, U.S. Embassy Charge d’Affaires
a5428.name: Joseph Zadrozny
a5428.title: U.S. Embassy Charge d’Affaires
a5428.speech: The release quotes him as highlighting America’s contribution to the Health Sector of Liberia for the well-being of its citizens nationwide ; reaffirmed America’s steadfast commitment to working with Liberia to identify ways to strengthen economic cooperation.

a5459.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
a5459.name: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
a5459.speech: Said lack of funding aggravated by President Donald Trump administration's cuts to foreign aid would hinder the supply of lifesaving food to treat 80,000 malnourished children in Nigeria within the next two months ; said 1.3 million children under the age of five suffering from severe acute malnutrition risk losing access to lifesaving support this year in Ethiopia and Nigeria.

a5459.speaker: Experts and nutrition focal organisations
a5459.name: Experts and nutrition focal organisations
a5459.speech: Harped on the need for urgent and holistic measures to address the menace; said the persistent malnutrition crisis in northern Nigeria stems from a variety of factors such as inflation, food insecurity, insufficient healthcare infrastructure, ongoing security issues and disease outbreaks compounded by low vaccine coverage.

a5459.speaker: Cristian Munduate, UNICEF Nigeria Representative
a5459.name: Cristian Munduate
a5459.title: UNICEF Nigeria Representative
a5459.speech: Said nearly 5.4 million under-five children in the North West and North East are suffering from acute malnutrition, with projections indicating an additional one million cases by April 2025 ; called on government to scale up nutrition interventions and promote child spacing initiatives to tackle the underlying challenge of rapid population growth.

a5459.speaker: Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) (statement)
a5459.name: Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) (statement)
a5459.speech: Said in 2024 its teams treated about 357,000 children suffering from malnutrition in the North: "This is an increase of 35 per cent compared to the 265,500 children treated in 2023. Among those treated in 2024, 75,000 required inpatient care, while 282,000 received outpatient treatment. In 2024, the surge in malnutrition cases began as early as March, well before the usual peak season in July, and extended through November, a time when cases are typically expected to decline. This situation raises fears that the severity of malnutrition in 2025 could exceed that of previous years."

a5459.speaker: Christos Christou, MSF international president
a5459.name: Christos Christou
a5459.title: MSF international president
a5459.speech: Said the numbers in 2022 and 2023 were already critically high, adding that between January to August 2024, MSF saw a 51% increase in admissions of children with severe malnutrition, compared to the same period the previous year; said MSF also treated 52,725 children with severe malnutrition across the North in the first eight months of last year ; speaking after his visit to MSF treatment centres in Maiduguri, Borno State: "Unvaccinated children are particularly vulnerable to vaccine-preventable diseases, which elevate the risk of acute malnutrition."

a5459.speaker: Save the Children International (SCI)
a5459.name: Save the Children International (SCI)
a5459.speech: Said without an urgent action, an additional one million children in Nigeria would be suffering from acute malnutrition by next month; said about 1.8 million could be experiencing Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM), representing an alarming 80% increase in SAM cases; said the situation is particularly dire in the North West and the North East where ongoing conflict and insecurity are driving displacement and disrupting livelihoods.

a5459.speaker: Cadre Harmonise hunger data analysis
a5459.name: Cadre Harmonise hunger data analysis
a5459.speech: Analysis of hunger data from Cadre Harmonise showed that 5.4 million children are at risk of facing acute malnutrition by April, a 25% increase compared to the 4.4 per cent last year April.

a5459.speaker: Duncan Harvey, Save the Children's Country Director for Nigeria
a5459.name: Duncan Harvey
a5459.title: Save the Children's Country Director for Nigeria
a5459.speech: "In Nigeria, the crisis is reaching unprecedented levels as catastrophic climate disasters, escalating insecurity, and soaring prices threaten to leave over 16 million children hungry. Urgent action is essential to combat this devastating and unacceptable trend of child hunger and malnutrition and ensure a brighter future for Nigeria's children."

a5459.speaker: Aisha, 27, mother of six, at Save the Children's clinic in Damaturu
a5459.name: Aisha
a5459.title: 27, mother of six, at Save the Children's clinic in Damaturu
a5459.speech: "Hunger has entered my daughter's body and she has emaciated terribly because I am unable to breastfeed her, I don't produce breast milk. It has affected her growth compared to other children. We are grateful to Save the Children for the support at the centre."

a5459.speaker: Hajara, 15, a child campaigner from Katsina
a5459.name: Hajara
a5459.title: 15, a child campaigner from Katsina
a5459.speech: "I am so worried about how food insecurity is hitting children in our community. With banditry everywhere, farmers cannot go to farms so food is getting harder to find. Lots of children go to bed hungry, and malnutrition level is high, leaving us tired and unable to concentrate in school. We need our leaders to step up, bring security back, and help us get the support we need so every child here can grow up safe, well-fed, and healthy."

a5459.speaker: Aisha Abdullahi, a school teacher and mother of five in Kano
a5459.name: Aisha Abdullahi
a5459.title: a school teacher and mother of five in Kano
a5459.speech: "Malnutrition among school-age children is a major risk factor for low school enrolment, high absenteeism, early dropouts, and unsatisfactory classroom performance. I am a mother and I take care of children in school. Malnourished children are more prone to infections and illnesses, which can lead to missed school days and falling behind in their education. Governments at all levels must rise to the occasion and address the problem. Children are the future of every society."

a5459.speaker: Murjanatu Bello from Gagi District, Sokoto State (caregiver)
a5459.name: Murjanatu Bello from Gagi District
a5459.title: Sokoto State (caregiver)
a5459.speech: "She initially started purging (diarrhoea). We took her to the nearest clinic where she was admitted for some days. Some days after we were discharged, we realised, she was losing weight and a woman from the neighbourhood advised that we should bring her to the clinic for a proper check-up. We then took her to Gagi clinic, where she was subjected to some tests and later confirmed to be suffering from severe malnourishment."

a5459.speaker: Umaima Abu from Bubare village (caregiver)
a5459.name: Umaima Abu from Bubare village (caregiver)
a5459.speech: "We spent a lot of money on traditional medicine without any improvement. We then decided to take him (her son) to the primary health centre, Gagi in Sokoto-South Local Government Area. He was given some drugs after which the health worker advised us to take him for Tamowa (malnutrition) test which we did. They put something on his hand and later told us our child was malnourished. They gave us the supplements free which we have been feeding him with. He is now recuperating."

a5459.speaker: Kulu Ardor from Lambo village in Kware Local Government Area (caregiver)
a5459.name: Kulu Ardor from Lambo village in Kware Local Government Area (caregiver)
a5459.speech: "He started losing weight; we spent some money treating him because we thought it was a different ailment, until we brought him to the hospital. We were given RUTF in the hospital which we were told was donated by one agency. We have been seeing some changes in him since he started taking it. He is getting well now."

a5459.speaker: Dr. Tushar Rane, UNICEF Chief of Borno Field Office
a5459.name: Dr. Tushar Rane
a5459.title: UNICEF Chief of Borno Field Office
a5459.speech: Said children in Borno, Yobe and Adamawa states are battling escalating levels of malnutrition and there is need for immediate and holistic response to address it; quoting the 2023 lean season Nutrition and Food Security Surveillance (NFSS) Round 13, he said the prevalence of global acute malnutrition (GAM) among children under five years in Borno was 10.2%, 8.0% in Yobe and 4.0% in Adamawa, and that an estimated 511,807 children under five suffer from Severe Acute Malnutrition annually ; "In our states, approximately 2.8 million children under five and pregnant and lactating women (PLWs) are in need of preventative nutrition services."

a5459.speaker: Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF)
a5459.name: Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF)
a5459.speech: Said over 40,000 children were treated for malnutrition in Kano State in 2024 ; advocated the establishment of outpatient feeding centres across all LGAs in Kano to enhance community-based management of malnutrition and reduce severe cases.

a5459.speaker: Hemmed Lukonge, MSF project coordinator in Kano State
a5459.name: Hemmed Lukonge
a5459.title: MSF project coordinator in Kano State
a5459.speech: "We are dealing with chronic and abnormal surge of severe acute malnutrition, children are coming from around 37 local government areas of Kano State and the state Ministry of Health does not have the necessary means in terms of nutrition supplies and human resources to address the matter."

a5459.speaker: Malama Umaima Bello, mother of one of the malnourished children at Unguwa Uku primary healthcare facility
a5459.name: Malama Umaima Bello
a5459.title: mother of one of the malnourished children at Unguwa Uku primary healthcare facility
a5459.speech: Said being at the facility had accorded her the chance to "understand the difference between food and nutritional food"; she linked malnutrition, especially in the North, to food insecurity, poverty, poor knowledge of healthy feeding and high prevalence of vaccine preventable childhood illnesses like measles.

a5459.speaker: Nutrition experts in Kano State
a5459.name: Nutrition experts in Kano State
a5459.speech: Said the main cause of food insecurity could be linked to decrease in agricultural activities due to climate change, high cost of living/high inflation rate.

a5459.speaker: Hajiya Rakiya Balarabe, Director of Nutrition, Kano State Ministry of Health
a5459.name: Hajiya Rakiya Balarabe
a5459.title: Director of Nutrition, Kano State Ministry of Health
a5459.speech: Said the state, in collaboration with various local and international agencies, is working to address malnutrition.

a5459.speaker: Rilwanu Mohammed, Executive Chairman of Bauchi State Primary Healthcare Development Board
a5459.name: Rilwanu Mohammed
a5459.title: Executive Chairman of Bauchi State Primary Healthcare Development Board
a5459.speech: Said N100 million had been earmarked for nutrition activities; said the Nigeria Demographic Health Survey 2023/2024 showed that the state had a high rate of malnourished children.

a5459.speaker: UNICEF report
a5459.name: UNICEF report
a5459.speech: About 300,000 children are malnourished in Sokoto State, according to a UNICEF report.

a5459.speaker: Miqdat Ibrahim, a service provider at Gagi PHC
a5459.name: Miqdat Ibrahim
a5459.title: a service provider at Gagi PHC
a5459.speech: Attributed the surge in malnutrition cases to insecurity and poverty: "Before the current economic and security issues, we were receiving between 70 and 135 cases, but the number increased significantly because of the presence of IDP camp in Gagi."

a5459.speaker: Christen Muduate, UNICEF Country Representative
a5459.name: Christen Muduate
a5459.title: UNICEF Country Representative
a5459.speech: Said 250,000 out of 1.2 million children in Zamfara were battling malnutrition; said one out of every 10 children in the state was staring at death, while stunting among children aged between 0 and five years was at an alarming rate of 45.2 per cent ; "In Zamfara, we are intending to treat 400,000 under five children suffering from Severe Acute Malnutrition. 200,000 additional children in the North-West will require Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) in 2025, compared to 2024."

a5459.speaker: Nkeiruka Enwelum, UNICEF's Nutrition Officer in Abuja
a5459.name: Nkeiruka Enwelum
a5459.title: UNICEF's Nutrition Officer in Abuja
a5459.speech: "Inadequate nutrition has lots of consequences on general health and wellbeing. There is also the implication of increased mortality, especially in children less than three years of age and in women of reproductive age as the main population groups of concern. The foods that we eat give us different things in our bodies. Failure to eat some of these things in the right quantities can result in poor growth and development in the body."

a5459.speaker: Nemat Hajeebhoy, Chief of Nutrition, UNICEF Nigeria
a5459.name: Nemat Hajeebhoy
a5459.title: Chief of Nutrition, UNICEF Nigeria
a5459.speech: Said investing in malnutrition translates to investing in brain development and the human capital of a country: "Therefore, it is absolutely vital and critical to our growth. If you have children and you don't feed them well, they will not be able to grow well."

a5459.speaker: Save the Children
a5459.name: Save the Children
a5459.speech: Called on governments to tackle food shortages, stabilise rising prices and increase protection for farmers facing violence from armed groups: "Governments also need to address the climate crisis by building communities' resilience, as well as more awareness and early warning for people to prepare for climate induced disasters."

a5459.speaker: Experts at MSF
a5459.name: Experts at MSF
a5459.speech: Urged strengthening healthcare facilities to diagnose and treat malnutrition, reinforcing vaccine programmes, enhancing access to nutritious food, improving water and sanitation, and raising awareness.

a5470.speaker: Mama Djombo, Guinean music group
a5470.name: Mama Djombo
a5470.title: Guinean music group
a5470.speech: sang: "Pikinu na tamanhu…ma garandi na fama" ("Small in size… but great in fame").

a5639.speaker: Bank of Mozambique (BdM) (data)
a5639.name: Bank of Mozambique (BdM) (data)
a5639.speech: According to data from the Bank of Mozambique, Mozambique imported rice equivalent to 4.1 billion meticais in the first quarter of this year alone, almost 15% of total consumer goods purchased abroad in the same period; in 2024 imports reached a historic record of 28.6 billion meticais, growth of 38.8% over the previous year.

a5639.speaker: National Institute of Statistics (INE) (data)
a5639.name: National Institute of Statistics (INE) (data)
a5639.speech: Data reveal that in 2023 the country produced only 161,829 tonnes of rice, a fall of 34% from the 245,792 tonnes of 2022, the lowest level of the last five years; Zambézia province led national production with 48,537 tonnes, followed by Gaza with 40,946.

a5804.speaker: United Nations
a5804.name: United Nations
a5804.speech: stated that the sovereign debt of African countries has reached 1 trillion US dollars.

a5804.speaker: Director General of Sonatrach (Algeria)
a5804.name: Director General of Sonatrach (Algeria)
a5804.speech: said in an interview with the media that the company he heads had signed 16 new export contracts in 2024. Sonatrach has mastered a number of new markets, exporting gas to Germany, the Czech Republic and Croatia, as well as crude oil to the countries of the Americas, India and Brazil.

a5804.speaker: Cameroon (government announcement)
a5804.name: Cameroon (government announcement)
a5804.speech: announced a competition for the design and construction of the Kikot Mbebe hydroelectric plant on the Sanaga River. The project is being carried out by the Kikot-Mbb Hydro Power Company.

a5924.speaker: TPLF / Tigray People's Liberation Front (statement)
a5924.name: TPLF / Tigray People's Liberation Front (statement)
a5924.speech: Announced in a recent statement that citizens displaced from their homes during the war in northern Ethiopia can return to where they were only when the territory of the Tigray region is restored to what it was; said that under the constitution the return of Tigray's displaced people is possible only when the region's territorial integrity and control over the areas it used to administer are restored, which requires that forces other than the national defence army withdraw from the Tigray region, so as to build trust, stabilise the region, and allow displaced citizens to return home in dignity and safety.

a5924.speaker: TPLF / Tigray People's Liberation Front (statement)
a5924.name: TPLF / Tigray People's Liberation Front (statement)
a5924.speech: Said that although the US Secretary of State described the changes and problems in the region, the claims that displaced citizens have returned home and that basic services have been restored do not reflect the reality on the ground, noting that no displaced people have returned to Western Tigray and that most of the displaced come from that area; said that while the silencing of the guns and the resumption of basic supplies may be called positive changes, the presence in Tigray of forces other than the national defence army is an obstacle preventing the displaced from returning.

a5924.speaker: TPLF / Tigray People's Liberation Front (statement)
a5924.name: TPLF / Tigray People's Liberation Front (statement)
a5924.speech: Asked that the international community participate in the transitional justice process, said a lasting solution must be found through meaningful and urgent political dialogue, and announced that it is ready for dialogue and for the Pretoria agreement to be implemented for the benefit of the community.

a5924.speaker: Antony Blinken, US Secretary of State (statement)
a5924.name: Antony Blinken
a5924.title: US Secretary of State (statement)
a5924.speech: Stated, marking the second anniversary of the halting of the war under the Pretoria agreement, that important changes have come to the Tigray region, that the sound of gunfire is no longer heard, that displaced people have returned to their homes and that basic supplies have begun to be provided; said in the statement that he welcomes the completion of the roadmap of the transitional justice policy process; asked that the Ethiopian government implement victim-centred transitional justice and that a credible national dialogue be conducted, and said political discussion should be held to resolve other conflicts seen in Ethiopia and that he is concerned about the growing conflict in the Amhara region.

a5924.speaker: Antony Blinken, US Secretary of State (phone call with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed)
a5924.name: Antony Blinken
a5924.title: US Secretary of State (phone call with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed)
a5924.speech: Discussed with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (PhD) by telephone a few days earlier the second anniversary of the Pretoria agreement, and it was stated that America would give its support to the Ethiopian government so that this agreement is successfully implemented.

a5977.speaker: Jeffrey Barbee, filmmaker
a5977.name: Jeffrey Barbee
a5977.title: filmmaker
a5977.speech: "I was amazed that the whole project had gone ahead in such a widespread way," Barbee told the Daily Maverick on Wednesday. "Everyone seemed surprised at my interest. When some realised I was a journalist they got very upset very quickly, and by and large no one had any idea what I was talking about regarding the dangers of this process." ; when Barbee spoke to journalists, community members, San activists and lawyers in Botswana, he found that the public was largely unaware that the gas exploration was taking place.

a5977.speaker: Keikabile Mogodu, San rights advocate
a5977.name: Keikabile Mogodu
a5977.title: San rights advocate
a5977.speech: "We have heard nothing. We are in the dark," he told the Guardian.

a5977.speaker: Jeff Ramsay, Botswana government spokesperson
a5977.name: Jeff Ramsay
a5977.title: Botswana government spokesperson
a5977.speech: Admitted that "Coal bed methane is being prospected in the country". He also said initially: "Environmental impact assessments and management plans are a legal requirement for all mining in our country."

a5977.speaker: Steve Boden, Sasol's unconventional gas development manager
a5977.name: Steve Boden
a5977.title: Sasol's unconventional gas development manager
a5977.speech: Allegedly told the Guardian: "We weren't required to do an environmental management plan for it but in our opinion it's best practice that we do."

a5977.speaker: Richard Lee, Communications Manager for the Open Society Initiative for Southern Africa (OSISA)
a5977.name: Richard Lee
a5977.title: Communications Manager for the Open Society Initiative for Southern Africa (OSISA)
a5977.speech: Believes that the government of Botswana's approach to the issue has been grossly remiss: "Given the scale of the developments in Botswana and the controversy surrounding the potential effects of unconventional natural gas production in South Africa, Europe and the USA, the government in Gaborone had a clear duty to inform the people - particularly communities that are living in or near the concessions - about gas developments. But they did not do it even though gas operations have been underway for years. The people of Botswana have the right to publicly debate issues of national importance like this and they have not had that opportunity."

a5977.speaker: Ministry of Minerals, Energy and Water Resources of Botswana (statement)
a5977.name: Ministry of Minerals
a5977.title: Energy and Water Resources of Botswana (statement)
a5977.speech: "There are currently no fracking operations going on in the country except exploration drilling by various exploration companies," it said.

a5977.speaker: Jeffrey Barbee, filmmaker
a5977.name: Jeffrey Barbee
a5977.title: filmmaker
a5977.speech: "I stood at a fracking operation, with pressure truck, chemical mixer, drill and water truck. All the trucks were older ones from the early days of drilling in the US," he told the Daily Maverick. "It was such an odd feeling to be standing in the middle of the Botswana wilderness looking at an operation just like the ones in my valley in Colorado."

a5977.speaker: Kalahari Energy website (article dated 9 July 2010)
a5977.name: Kalahari Energy website (article dated 9 July 2010)
a5977.speech: "This week Exxaro Coal Botswana commenced with the perforation and fracturing of their 5-spot wells which will take them until mid-September to complete. Expertise has been sought from the USA for this programme, which consists of perforating the well's steel production casing with explosive charges followed by the fracturing of the coals with high pressure water, sand and chemicals."

a5977.speaker: Kalahari Energy website (article dated 15 August 2005)
a5977.name: Kalahari Energy website (article dated 15 August 2005)
a5977.speech: Explains that water evaporation ponds are under construction: "Initially the ponds will be used to hold the water for hydraulic fracturing of the wells."

a5977.speaker: Botswana government (second statement, late Wednesday)
a5977.name: Botswana government (second statement
a5977.title: late Wednesday)
a5977.speech: Said it stood by its earlier statement that "there are currently no fracking operations going on in the country except exploration drilling", then added a caveat: "No current operations have been given permission to conduct hydraulic fracking...Permission has, however, been given in some instances in the past for the use of industrial explosives in sub-surface fracturing, which some may view as a type of 'fracking'." The government also said that this year there has been "a significant decline" on prospecting concessions in the CKGR ; the government's riposte is that all "processes and procedures involving mineral licensing" sit as public documents on its own website.

a5977.speaker: Richard Lee, Communications Manager for OSISA
a5977.name: Richard Lee
a5977.title: Communications Manager for OSISA
a5977.speech: "The government's claim that gas operations are still at the exploration stage is a smokescreen to cover up the fact that the story has come out. One geologist told us that they had been flaring gas for two years in one location. Surely the government has a duty to inform people about that, even if it is only exploration?"

a5977.speaker: Global Visionary award organisers (press release)
a5977.name: Global Visionary award organisers (press release)
a5977.speech: Put out a press release paying tribute to President Ian Khama's government for "piloting pan-African efforts to monitor and safeguard water, minerals, and wildlife - all of which are crucial to future conservation efforts".

a5977.speaker: International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN)
a5977.name: International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN)
a5977.speech: Awarded Khama a lifetime honorary membership for his "life-long commitment to the environment".

a5977.speaker: Richard Lee, Communications Manager for OSISA
a5977.name: Richard Lee
a5977.title: Communications Manager for OSISA
a5977.speech: "This expose puts [the government's] reputation at risk, since the authorities have been handing out concessions inside, and in the buffer zones alongside, globally renowned and biodiversity-rich parks. The government needs to rapidly explain this contradiction to its own people and the international community."

a5977.speaker: Botswana government website (map of concessions)
a5977.name: Botswana government website (map of concessions)
a5977.speech: A map on the government's website indicating the distribution of concessions given to multinational energy companies reveals that a good chunk of the Central Kalahari Game Reserve (CKGR) is covered, and it appears that part of the Chobe National Park is too. Among the companies given permission to drill for coal bed methane are SASOL, Anglo American, Exxaro, Kalahari Energy and others.

a6261.speaker: Joel Sauane, expert of the Conecta Negócios project
a6261.name: Joel Sauane
a6261.title: expert of the Conecta Negócios project
a6261.speech: Speaking to AIM on Wednesday during a supervision mission in Nampula, said the project has already reached important milestones in its implementation: “The training process is progressing in Nampula, Tete and Cabo Delgado provinces, which are the priorities, with the support of the Northern Integrated Development Agency (ADIN) as the project's co-implementing entity.”

a6261.speaker: Joel Sauane, expert of the Conecta Negócios project
a6261.name: Joel Sauane
a6261.title: expert of the Conecta Negócios project
a6261.speech: Explained that the training is aimed at instructing the SMEs on how to establish connections with the megaproject operators and the customers in general: “In the first phase, SMEs receive training in business management, gender inclusion, green competitiveness, and digital skills. In the second phase, they move on to the ISO 9001 certification process, required to supply goods and services to megaprojects, and can then apply for grants.”

a6261.speaker: Joel Sauane, expert of the Conecta Negócios project
a6261.name: Joel Sauane
a6261.title: expert of the Conecta Negócios project
a6261.speech: Revealed that the overall goal is to train 9,000 SMEs, of which 6,000 have already been trained, that the project intends to cover 3,000 SMEs in Nampula and so far 2,900 have been covered, and added: “In order to support these companies financally, 15 million dollars in grants are available, divided equally into 7.5 million for microenterprises and 7.5 million for SMEs.”

a6261.speaker: Hegínio Mussequece, business owner in the construction sector, Nampula
a6261.name: Hegínio Mussequece
a6261.title: business owner in the construction sector, Nampula
a6261.speech: “We learned tools focused on results. Our hope is to obtain certification that will allow us to participate in major projects underway in Nampula province and beyond. We intend to apply for the grant to leverage our business with the acquisition of equipment.”

a6261.speaker: Linda Nhalate, business owner in the seafood industry
a6261.name: Linda Nhalate
a6261.title: business owner in the seafood industry
a6261.speech: Praised the management skills learned in the training, claiming that they “will help us implement more professional administrative procedures” ; “This will help the company grow. We hope to continue expanding and recruiting more young people as now we are hiring 12 permanent employees and 40 seasonal employees.”

a6334.speaker: Keda Ballah, CILSS Coordinating Minister and Chad's Minister of Agricultural Production and Industrialisation
a6334.name: Keda Ballah
a6334.title: CILSS Coordinating Minister and Chad's Minister of Agricultural Production and Industrialisation
a6334.speech: In opening the meeting he first wished to express all his gratitude to Brigadier General Abdourahamane Tiani, President of the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland (CNSP), for the facilities granted to CILSS for the smooth running of this important conference. ; He finally reiterated his thanks to the Nigerien authorities, to the organisers of the conference, and to all the technical and financial partners of CILSS, notably the European Union, USAID, the World Bank and all the scientific and technical partners who have always stood alongside CILSS in facing the many development challenges confronting the countries of the Sahel.

a6334.speaker: Keda Ballah, CILSS Coordinating Minister and Chad's Minister of Agricultural Production and Industrialisation
a6334.name: Keda Ballah
a6334.title: CILSS Coordinating Minister and Chad's Minister of Agricultural Production and Industrialisation
a6334.speech: He set out the regional context in which the conference is taking place, “a context characterised by a resurgence of extreme climate events, notably devastating floods, and an almost structural and increasingly worrying food and nutrition insecurity affecting nearly 28 million Sahelians and West Africans.” ; “Recent CILSS studies and the latest report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) have shown that sub-Saharan Africa in general, and West Africa in particular, is considered one of the regions of the world most vulnerable to the perverse effects of climate change, which manifest themselves in extreme weather and climate phenomena such as those we are currently experiencing.” ; “The region is recording exceptional rains this year, destroying everything in their path. As a result, our civil protection and other humanitarian services are currently hard at work in our respective countries trying to provide various forms of assistance to victims and disaster-stricken people.”

a6334.speaker: Recent CILSS studies and the latest IPCC report
a6334.name: Recent CILSS studies and the latest IPCC report
a6334.speech: Have shown that sub-Saharan Africa in general, and West Africa in particular, is considered one of the regions of the world most vulnerable to the perverse effects of climate change, which manifest themselves in extreme weather and climate phenomena.

a6334.speaker: Keda Ballah, CILSS Coordinating Minister and Chad's Minister of Agricultural Production and Industrialisation
a6334.name: Keda Ballah
a6334.title: CILSS Coordinating Minister and Chad's Minister of Agricultural Production and Industrialisation
a6334.speech: He announced that “efforts have been undertaken and continue to be carried out by our States to adapt to climate change and thus contribute to reducing greenhouse gases, without however obtaining the expected results in terms of resilience.” ; He stressed that adaptation options and strategies have been identified but are still struggling to be implemented because of a number of constraints the sub-region has identified, citing the insufficiency and compartmentalisation of structural regional investment projects for adaptation, the weak consideration of adaptation and resilience issues in public policy and planning documents at all scales, the weakness of technological adaptation capacities, the weakness of capacities to mobilise external resources (climate funds, development partner funds), and the weakness of capacities to assess losses and damages caused by climate shocks.

a6334.speaker: Keda Ballah, CILSS Coordinating Minister and Chad's Minister of Agricultural Production and Industrialisation
a6334.name: Keda Ballah
a6334.title: CILSS Coordinating Minister and Chad's Minister of Agricultural Production and Industrialisation
a6334.speech: “More than ever, our sub-region needs broad cooperation and solidarity between our regional institutions, between our States and between our research institutions in order to anticipate these climate-related risks and better prepare our communities to cope with climate variability and change.” ; “Also, we must work to significantly improve our public policies on the management of natural disaster crises, which will become increasingly recurrent.” ; “We must put in place, each according to its own specificities, technical and political mechanisms dedicated to the management of natural disasters and involving all stakeholders.” ; “I dare to hope that this conference will seal, on the one hand, the synergy of actions between our regional institutions, researchers, civil society organisations and policy makers, and will lay the foundations for a framework of regional scientific cooperation on climate in order to strengthen the resilience of the populations of West Africa on the one hand and those of the Sahel on the other.”

a6334.speaker: Colonel Elhadj Ousmane Mahaman, Niger's Minister of Agriculture and Livestock
a6334.name: Colonel Elhadj Ousmane Mahaman
a6334.title: Niger's Minister of Agriculture and Livestock
a6334.speech: Welcomed his guests before conveying to them the greetings of the Head of State, Brigadier General Abdourahamane Tiani, and of Prime Minister Ali Mahaman Lamine Zeine. ; He also welcomed the relevance of the theme chosen for this 3rd edition of the conference, in that “the sub-region has in recent years faced a resurgence of extreme climate hazards with harmful effects on our environment, our food security and our populations.” ; He mentioned the diversity of initiatives undertaken at national, regional and international level to support States in coping with climate hazards, notably citing the one aimed at providing the different regions of Africa with a regional climate centre led by the World Meteorological Organization.

a6334.speaker: Several speakers at the opening ceremony
a6334.name: Several speakers at the opening ceremony
a6334.speech: Took turns to salute and congratulate CILSS for this important initiative before wishing every success to the work of this 3rd conference.

a6355.speaker: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) from across the continent
a6355.name: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) from across the continent
a6355.speech: have renewed calls for the cancellation of unsustainable and illegitimate debts to enable African nations to prioritise development and invest in their people and economies.

a6355.speaker: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
a6355.name: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
a6355.speech: urged reforms to global financial institutions, accusing them of perpetuating colonial-era debt systems and deepening economic inequalities.

a6355.speaker: African Forum and Network on Debt and Development (AFRODAD) and partner organisations (joint statement)
a6355.name: African Forum and Network on Debt and Development (AFRODAD) and partner organisations (joint statement)
a6355.speech: In a joint statement, the organisations voiced support for the establishment of an African Credit Rating Agency, aimed at providing fairer assessments of African economies and reducing the inflated risk premiums imposed by international credit rating agencies: “We support the establishment of the African Credit Rating Agency to create sustainable solutions for Africa’s access to affordable capital, currently burdened by high-risk premiums placed by international agencies,” the statement read.

a6355.speaker: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
a6355.name: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
a6355.speech: also championed the development of a United Nations Framework Convention on Sovereign Debt during the upcoming Fourth Financing for Development Conference in Seville, Spain, proposing it as a viable alternative to the existing international financial and debt systems.

a6355.speaker: African Forum and Network on Debt and Development (AFRODAD) and partner organisations
a6355.name: African Forum and Network on Debt and Development (AFRODAD) and partner organisations
a6355.speech: While acknowledging Africa’s significant strides in political, economic, health, education, environmental, innovation, and cultural sectors, the organisations emphasised that the fight for genuine debt and economic freedom remained ongoing.

a6355.speaker: African Forum and Network on Debt and Development (AFRODAD)
a6355.name: African Forum and Network on Debt and Development (AFRODAD)
a6355.speech: According to AFRODAD, Africa’s total public debt had now surpassed US$1.8 trillion, with at least 34 African countries spending more on external debt repayments than on healthcare and education.

a6355.speaker: AFRODAD and partner organisations (joint statement)
a6355.name: AFRODAD and partner organisations (joint statement)
a6355.speech: The statement noted that private creditors, often motivated by profit and harsh credit ratings, lend to African nations at significantly higher rates than official creditors — driving debt servicing costs to approximately US$90 billion annually.

a6355.speaker: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
a6355.name: Civil Society Organisations (CSOs)
a6355.speech: “The continent faces a substantial development financing gap, averaging US$200 billion per year, which threatens the successful attainment of both the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030 and Agenda 2063,” the CSOs noted. ; They further criticised the global debt and financial system, describing it as one shaped by market liberalism, creditor dominance, and resource extraction — calling for structural reforms to better serve Africa’s development needs.

a6451.speaker: Elon Musk (post on his social media platform X)
a6451.name: Elon Musk (post on his social media platform X)
a6451.speech: “To be clear, I am NOT taking drugs!” ; “The New York Times was lying their ass off.”

a6451.speaker: The New York Times (investigation)
a6451.name: The New York Times (investigation)
a6451.speech: Reported he was using drugs, particularly the psychedelic-inducing drug ketamine, while he was on the campaign trail with President Donald Trump.

a6451.speaker: Elon Musk (to The New York Times)
a6451.name: Elon Musk (to The New York Times)
a6451.speech: “I tried prescription ketamine a few years ago and said so on X, so this [is] not even news. It helps for getting out of dark mental holes, but I haven't taken it since then.”

a6451.speaker: Elon Musk (to The Don Lemon Show)
a6451.name: Elon Musk (to The Don Lemon Show)
a6451.speech: Said “he gets a prescription from a real doctor”, but did not confirm whether he takes the medicine in the presence of doctors, only that he takes “a small amount of ketamine every other week” with “several weeks going buy where I don't use it”.

a6451.speaker: Peer-reviewed research (pooled study of dozens of studies)
a6451.name: Peer-reviewed research (pooled study of dozens of studies)
a6451.speech: Shows that ketamine, when used in combination with other antidepressants, could help even the most treatment-resistant depression patients to lift their mood.

a6451.speaker: Psychiatrists (told Bhekisisa)
a6451.name: Psychiatrists (told Bhekisisa)
a6451.speech: Told Bhekisisa that the ketamine nasal spray, approved in 2022 for treatment-resistant depression, isn't available in the country.

a6451.speaker: South African Society of Psychiatrists (Sasop) guidelines
a6451.name: South African Society of Psychiatrists (Sasop) guidelines
a6451.speech: Has published guidelines for ketamine's use for the treatment of depression, including that it's only used for treatment-resistant depression, and only in drip-form, so not as an intramuscular injection or as a tablet that dissolves under the tongue; ketamine also has to be given by an anaesthetist or a GP with a diploma in anaesthetics “in an environment where it is possible to monitor the patient and potentially resuscitate”.

a6451.speaker: Bhekisisa's TV programme Health Beat (investigation)
a6451.name: Bhekisisa's TV programme Health Beat (investigation)
a6451.speech: Found many “cowboy clinics” where unqualified workers give ketamine to people with depression and for conditions such as attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder, for which there isn't credible evidence that it works.

a6451.speaker: Boitumelo Semete-Makokotlela, chief executive of the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (Sahpra)
a6451.name: Boitumelo Semete-Makokotlela
a6451.title: chief executive of the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (Sahpra)
a6451.speech: “[Although off-label use] is an informed decision, on published clinical evidence, [it's important to remember] that it means that if anything happens to a patient, they [patients or healthcare providers] then cannot hold the manufacturer responsible when it, in fact, registered the product for a different indication.”

a6451.speaker: Experts (unnamed)
a6451.name: Experts (unnamed)
a6451.speech: Say unregulated use of ketamine is not only risky — it can be deadly, because if someone takes too much of it, it can raise their blood pressure, make it hard to breathe and, among other things, cause seizures.

a6451.speaker: Authorities in Los Angeles (autopsy findings)
a6451.name: Authorities in Los Angeles (autopsy findings)
a6451.speech: Found that Friends actor Matthew Perry died in 2024 of what authorities called the “acute effects” of ketamine abuse, which was administered intravenously.

a6451.speaker: Bavi Vythilingum, psychiatrist and member of the South African Society of Psychiatrists
a6451.name: Bavi Vythilingum
a6451.title: psychiatrist and member of the South African Society of Psychiatrists
a6451.speech: On why psychiatrists are talking about ketamine now: “It's probably the first completely novel antidepressant that we've had for a long time. So with antidepressants, it usually takes about, say, two to three weeks for it to work. With ketamine, you can get a response within two to three days, and sometimes, as we give the infusion, patients feel better.” ; on why it works so fast: “We're not 100% sure, but we think that it's because it's working on the glutamate receptor and causes very big neurodevelopmental changes very rapidly, and that's what gives you that rapid onset of action” ; “Glutamate is a brain neurotransmitter like serotonin and noradrenaline. Glutamate is situated throughout the brain and ketamine works on that receptor.”

a6451.speaker: Bavi Vythilingum, psychiatrist and member of the South African Society of Psychiatrists
a6451.name: Bavi Vythilingum
a6451.title: psychiatrist and member of the South African Society of Psychiatrists
a6451.speech: “If you're taking ketamine, for example, for drug use, it would produce an altered state of consciousness, which can make you feel good, but can also be unpleasant. But certainly, for depression, it seems to work for a lot of people.”

a6451.speaker: Bavi Vythilingum, psychiatrist and member of the South African Society of Psychiatrists
a6451.name: Bavi Vythilingum
a6451.title: psychiatrist and member of the South African Society of Psychiatrists
a6451.speech: On who gets ketamine: “So there are two groups of people who would get ketamine: people who are extremely depressed, extremely suicidal and a danger to themselves, where we need a very rapid onset of action. And the second group of people are what we call treatment resistant, where they have failed what we call an adequate trial. So that's a trial at a high enough dose for a long enough period of time of two standard antidepressants.”

a6451.speaker: Bavi Vythilingum, psychiatrist and member of the South African Society of Psychiatrists
a6451.name: Bavi Vythilingum
a6451.title: psychiatrist and member of the South African Society of Psychiatrists
a6451.speech: On what patients experience: “Most people who have ketamine will have what we call a non-ordinary state of consciousness where they may feel they are not in their body, which is what we call dissociation. They may experience reality in different ways. They may see complex shapes and colours. They may feel sounds as being colours. It can be a beautiful experience, but it can also be an anxiety-provoking experience.” ; on duration: “For as long as we give the infusion. So usually about 40 minutes.
